name: Piedmont Players Theatre
bio: Piedmont Players Theatre (PPT) is a premier community theatre recognized for its commitment to excellence in theatrical production, education, and community engagement. Over its rich history, PPT has been a cornerstone of local arts and culture.

name: Little Theatre of Winston-Salem
bio:
PIEDMONT TRIAD'S OLDEST THEATRICAL ORGANIZATION

The Little Theatre of Winston-Salem is the oldest theatrical organization in the Piedmont Triad. For over 90 years audiences have experienced our spectacular productions!

As a fundamental part of Winston-Salem's cultural scene, we invite everyone in the community to exercise their imaginations, stretch their creative muscles, and experience the transformative magic of live theatre.

name: RSVP Community Theatre
bio:
RSVP Community Theatre traces its roots back to 1986. RSVP Community Theatre serves the community by bringing a variety of entertainment lovingly done. In operation for 33 years, music, drama, and comedy have been offered abundantly to Asheboro/Randolph County audiences, actors, and technicians. Learn more on Facebook at RSVP Community Theatre.

If you have questions, please call 336-625-8373.

name: Community Theatre of Greensboro
bio:
Founded in 1949, the Community Theatre of Greensboro is the oldest Arts organization in Guilford County.

What sets CTG apart? Our focus on reaching out to our entire community and concentrating on our mission:

Bringing our diverse community together to learn about, experience, and celebrate the joys of theatre.

Our goal is to help everyone in our community share in the excitement of participating in theatre—as actors, backstage crew, or audience members. We cherish diversity and non-traditional casting is a priority for us.

name: Kernersville Little Theatre
bio:
An insert in the program for Kernersville Little Theatre’s (KLT) first show read, “The concept of KLT was discussed for several years by different factions within the community. A grant from the Urban Arts Council of Winston-Salem made the dream a possibility.” And with that, community theatre in Kernersville, North Carolina was born.

With careful planning and unwavering dedication from a key group of individuals, KLT produced its first show, You Can’t Take It With You, in July 1977. Since then, hundreds of shows have been produced. Currently, we present four different shows in each September-June season.
The mission of Kernersville Little Theatre is to provide an avenue for development in all aspects of theatrical arts for all within the community and to provide entertainment for the community by offering a series of well-staged performances of live theater.

And while KLT does not have a permanent home for our productions, that has never stopped us from making sure the show goes on. We’ll be sure to let you know where you can find us throughout Kernersville.

As a non-profit, all-volunteer organization, KLT has been fortunate over so many years to have the support from those within the Kernersville community and around the Triad. We continue to have volunteers who have been with us from the very beginning, creating a strong sense of family. We are always welcoming new volunteers to our family and anxious to have you “Come Play With Us”.

name: Stained Glass Playhouse
bio:
Stained Glass Playhouse is a non-profit community theatre specializing in affordable, professional-quality productions in a small, intimate setting. 

Located in the former sanctuary of Marvin United Methodist Church in Winston-Salem, North Carolina, Stained Glass Playhouse offers productions and theatrical events which encompass moral messages, family values, and community issues.

name: Lee Street Theatre
bio:
Lee Street theatre was established in 2008 with the original goal of presenting alternative forms of performance art to the community. 

In the years that have followed, the company has lived up to this goal and become known for the diverse styles of programming offered, including one-act play festivals, original ten-minute play festivals, off-broadway style musicals and revues, reader’s theatre, of dance performances, original plays, variety shows, live music, and improvisational comedy. Showing a dedication to new playwrights, of the more than eighty programs that have been offered, Lee Street theatre has produced three full length, sixty ten-minute, and five one-act world premiere plays.

For 4 years, Lee Street theatre rented the black box theatre at the Looking Glass Artists Center for performances. In September 2012, Lee Street theatre embarked on its first ever Capital Campaign to build a new performing arts center in Downtown Salisbury. Construction was completed in November of 2013 and the Lee Street Theatre & Performing Arts Center at the Tom & Martha Smith Event Center has been a leader in the revitalization of the ‘Railwalk Arts District’ in Downtown Salisbury.

name: Palmetto Theatre of Walnut Cove
bio: The Palmetto Theatre of Walnut Cove traces its story to Jesse Booth, a local visionary and businessman who opened Walnut Cove's first movie theater in the 1930s inside a former garage at the corner of Third and Main streets, where it operated until 1949. The Palmetto name came back to town with W.D. Sands, who traveled with his father to Palmetto, Florida, to buy produce to sell around Walnut Cove and Danbury; Sands still recalls a sellout crowd in the old garage. Booth opened a second theater in King in 1938, which he later sold, and in 1949 opened the Palmetto on Main Street. For many Stokes County residents it was where they saw their first movies, from Gone with the Wind to World War II newsreels and Tom and Jerry cartoons, and its stage also hosted live music, wrestling, burlesque and visiting western film stars, with performers including Bill Monroe and the Blue Grass Boys, Ernest Tubb and his Troubadours, Red Sovine, Lash LaRue and Fuzzy Jones. Generations of couples met there and families spent evenings together in its seats. Television cut into movie audiences in the late 1950s and early 1960s, and in 1966 the Palmetto closed and was sold. Over the next fifty years the building served as an automobile dealership, a carpet store, an auto repair shop, a license plate agency and a storage space before falling into disrepair, with broken windows, missing doors and a collapsed roof that sheltered birds, bats and rats. Just one inspection away from condemnation, it was bought by six local citizens determined to save it, and with the help of many contributors and volunteers, and support from NC Rep. Kyle Hall, the restored Palmetto at 329 N. Main Street once again shines as a home for concerts, comedy, film screenings and community events.

name: High Point Community Theatre
bio: High Point Community Theatre is a volunteer-based arts organization dedicated to providing community involvement opportunities, inspiring appreciation for dramatic arts, and educating the next generation.

name: The Uwharrie Players
bio: The Uwharrie Players has been the community theater organization of Stanly County for over five decades. The Uwharrie Players was formed in the spring of 1975 as an outgrowth of the Stanly County Arts Council. Thirty-four charter members set out to establish a vehicle that would provide local citizens an opportunity to perform onstage and expose Stanly County to quality theatrical entertainment.

name: Davidson Community Players
bio: Davidson Community Players (DCP) produces theater that entertains, enriches, and fosters community involvement. As a non-profit, DCP prioritizes local talent, inclusivity, and affordable access. We believe theater serves a vital civic role, enhancing empathy, collaboration, and cultural understanding. Through diverse programming and education, DCP aims to be a joyful, supportive community pillar.

name: Raleigh Little Theatre
bio: Our Mission RLT is a welcoming community using theatre to enrich, educate, entertain and engage volunteers, students and audiences of all ages. Our Vision Performance: To offer innovative, engaging and diverse theatre and education.

name: Greenwood Community Theatre
bio:
Greenwood Community Theatre (GCT) is located at 110 Main Street in beautiful Uptown Greenwood, South Carolina. GCT aspires to enrich our community by creating and fostering professionalism and diversity in all its theatrical endeavors and experiences.

GCT reopened in January 2007 after an extensive 1.2 million dollar renovation project. Centrally located in the Emerald Triangle Cultural Arts District, GCT boasts a healthy offering of theatre, musical theatre, comedy, dramas, classic films, Indie films, music concerts and many rentals to local and touring organizations and businesses.

Our primary focus is to create theatre "for the community and by the community."


Theatre is a wonderful place for families to work together or to develop a new "theatre family". GCT believes in inclusiveness and nurturing each individual’s creative gifts and talents.

GCT is also home to the Penguin Project, which nourishes differently-abled young artists by providing the opportunity to star in a musical.

The Greenwood Community Theatre, Inc. is a non-profit 501(c)3 governed by a Board of Directors and managed by a Staff.

name: Town Theatre
bio:
“A stage society has been organized in Columbia for the purpose of encouraging and developing musical, vocal, and dramatic talent in this city and to furnish entertainment to those who enjoy these things but do not care to take an active part in them.”

Letter dated Jun 25, 1919 by John D. Neal
First Secretary of The Columbia Stage Society

Thus began a run of family-oriented entertainment at Town Theatre that continues to thrive today. The founders of the Town Theatre were not professional producers, directors or actors. They were a group of families who dreamed of a new concept for Columbia: a theatre where they and their families could not only watch plays, but also take part in them for fun and learn from the experience.

This commitment to presenting plays and musicals of wide general appeal has earned Town Theatre the largest regular audience of any cultural performing organization in Columbia. In fact, each season brings in close to 30,000 theatre patrons of all ages.

The actual Town Theatre building was constructed in 1924. It is the oldest communitytheatre building in continuous use in the United States and is listed in the National Register of Historic Places. Town Theatre has one of the largest auditoriums of any Columbia theatre group.

In 1993 the theatre unveiled a $1.2 million renovation which included opening the lobby completely to its two-story height to highlight the famous front arched window; improving backstage facilities for the actors and stage crew; and installing a counterweighted rigging system used in professional theatres that allows scenery to “fly” in and out from the loft, speeding up scene changes and allowing for more variety in stage backdrops.

Town Theatre provides an exceptional opportunity for entry level actors by giving them the chance to work on stage with experienced veterans, many of whom are working professionals volunteering their time. Many of Town Theatre’s current and alumni performers have appeared on Broadway, network television and in major feature films. They include Cats, A Chorus Line, Ruthless People, Hill Street Blues, and North and South.

Every performance has open auditions, with all community members being encouraged to attend. There is also ample opportunity for members of the community to get involved behind the scenes. The Columbia Stage Society offers opportunity and experience in theatre to its members, many of whom participate not only as actors but as costumers, set and backstage crew, as well as helping in the box office, or as ushers and house managers.

name: Three Bone Theatre
bio:
Three Bone Theatre is Charlotte's home for the best of adult contemporary theatre.
Our name is inspired by the Reba McEntire quote:
​"To succeed in life, you need three things; a wishbone, a backbone, and a funny bone."
We are known for our strong track record of fiscal responsibility, ambitious artistic excellence, a steadfast commitment to equity, both on and off the stage, and meaningful community partnerships.

Our Mission
To use great theatre as a catalyst for conversation and change in the community.
Our Vision
To create performing arts experiences that are socially engaged, professionally managed, and creatively inspired.

Our Policies
Three Bone Theatre is committed to modeling diversity, equity and inclusion for the entire arts industry of the nonprofit sector, and to maintaining an inclusive environment with equitable treatment for all. The following policies were adopted by our Board of Directors in September 2018. Every artist, volunteer, staff member and board member is required to accept and adhere to these policies. Click the links below to review the full documents.

Diversity, Equity and Inclusion Commitment
No-Harassment Policy
Privacy Policy
​
Our Commitment to Equity and Accessibility
Three Bone Theatre is committed to being an anti-racist, inclusive and accessible theatre company.
Please visit our Equity Initiatives page to learn more about our priorities and action plan.

If you have any questions or requests related to accessibility, please contact Robin Tynes-Miller, our Accessibility Coordinator, at Robin@threebonetheatre.com or call 704-559-9051.

Community Partners
We partner with a different local organization for each production with the hope of raising awareness to the unique themes present in each production and the commendable work that is being done in the Charlotte community. Visit our Community Partnerships page to learn more about our current and past partners.

name: Hendersonville Theatre
bio:
Mission Statement
Hendersonville Theatre’s mission is to enrich our community by serving as a beacon of the performing arts, inspiring, empowering, and educating through engaging in transformative experiences.

Vision
Become the premier professional-quality, progressive, and inclusive community theatre in WNC.

Organizational Values
Inclusion and Diversity: Hendersonville Theatre is dedicated to breaking down barriers and fostering inclusion and diversity by creating a safe, accessible, and empathetic environment where everyone is respected and valued.
Financial Responsibility: We value financial sustainability by maintaining efficient operations and a balanced budget supported by diverse revenue streams.
Education: We promote lifelong learning in the performing arts by nurturing knowledge, skills, and values as vital tools for personal and community enrichment.
Artistic Ambition: We embrace bold creative choices, artistic excellence, and innovative practices that elevate the artists and the community we serve.
Quality: Hendersonville Theatre upholds the highest standards of quality and professionalism, delivering excellence and lasting value that our audiences can rely on.
Community Leadership and Development: Hendersonville Theatre commits to leading through community collaboration, creative partnerships, and cultural enrichment. We strive for a positive economic impact that fosters a vibrant, engaged community.

name: Union County Playmakers
bio:
Mission & History
Our theatre is a beloved cultural hub for both locals and visitors alike. Founded in 2012, our mission is to provide a platform for artists and performers to share their talent with the community and to bring the joy of live performance to our region. We are proud to showcase a diverse range of productions, from classic plays and musicals to original works and modern interpretations. Our dedicated team of volunteers works tirelessly to bring these productions to life and to make sure that every performance is a memorable and enjoyable experience. We hope to see you at one of our shows soon!

Leadership
Effective leadership is crucial for any community theater group, and this includes the board of directors. The Union County Playmakers board is made up of individuals who are committed to the organization’s mission and have the skills and experience to guide it towards success. 

Community
The Union County Playmakers strive to have a positive impact on our community and this includes working with youth theatre, education and schools, and programing for senior citizens.

name: Burning Coal Theatre Company
bio:
Established 1997
Burning Coal’s mission is to produce literate, visceral, affecting theatre that is experienced, not simply seen.

We emphasize works that are experienced viscerally, unlike more traditional, linear plays where audiences are most often asked to observe without participating. Using the best local, national and international artists available, we produce explosive re-examinations of overlooked classics, modern classic and new plays that address ideas important to our community. With this in mind, we strive to achieve high-energy performances with minimalist production values.

Burning Coal was founded by Artistic Director Jerome Davis and Managing Director Simmie Kastner. It began as an itinerant company, performing in spaces across the Raleigh area. In 2008, Burning Coal finished the renovation of the historic Murphey School Auditorium in downtown Raleigh.

name: Studio 1
bio:
Our Story
Studio 1 is a performing arts center with an intimate 100-seat black box theatre located in Holly Hill Mall in Burlington, North Carolina. We are a dynamic community theatre group that focuses on providing unique programming in a positive atmosphere with professional results. We provide opportunities to performers of all ages, interests, experience levels and we offer training through classes and outreach.

Mission
Studio 1 is a community that understands the unique growth that occurs when we come together to do something bigger than ourselves. We build this community through compassionate inclusion, a spirit of empowerment, and the preservation of a theatre environment that celebrates the best in people.

Vision
Studio 1 strives to build and inspire citizens of tomorrow through visceral performances, thought-provoking content, an immersive theatre experience, and transformative, performing arts education.

Unique: Theatre has always been a place to make us think differently, laugh bigger, and challenge the status quo. We want to bring new and fresh content to our community while honoring and learning from the legendary.

Positive: Community is maintained with a culture of seeing the best in all of us. We strive to create an environment that is built on encouragement, inclusion, and acceptance.

Empowering: Through the performing arts, we grow and stretch our own abilities. Taking risks in the classroom and on stage makes us better people. Through mentorship and collaboration, we give our community permission to take those risks.

name: Hickory Community Theatre
bio:
The Hickory Community Theatre had its humble beginning in 1948 when the Hickory Recreation Department employed Kay Johnson to form a theatre group. Her first offering was a series of radio dramas aired on WIRC. In 1949, informal meetings, encouraged by the Kramer family, led to the formation of what was then known as The Hickory Little Theatre. The HLT first production was an evening of one-act plays, so successful that the company presented its first full-length production, YOU CAN'T TAKE IT WITH YOU in October in the auditorium at City Hall. The building has been the home of HCT ever since.

The Theatre grew in popularity and community support through the ’50s and staged its first musical production, THE BOYFRIEND, in 1958 – the same year that Charles Jeffers started his life-long involvement with HCT.
A new city hall was built in 1976 and HCT slowly moved into more of the old building. Renovations in 1984 led to the two performance spaces known to modern audiences, the extremely popular Firemen’s Kitchen and the HCT Mainstage, which the City Council renamed The Charles E. Jeffers Theatre in 1988, when the City turned over the entire building to the use of the Theatre. Renovations continued in the 1990s that completed the exterior restoration of the building and renovations to the Charles E. Jeffers Theatre. 

Each year, HCT and its community of volunteers celebrate its yearlong season of productions, events, and activities with the Kay Awards ceremony. “The Kays” honor the volunteers who have labored and shared their talents to support the Theatre throughout the year.  The awards, named in honor of Kay Johnson are hosted by the Guild at HCT.

The Guild represents the highest level of volunteerism at HCT. Guild members, in addition to their individual volunteer service, collectively complete projects to improve the appeal and function of the Theatre and conduct special fundraisers for purchase of needed equipment. 

Charles Jeffers, Managing Artistic Director since 1960, officially retired from his full-time duties in 2000. Pamela Livingstone was chosen as the new Managing Artistic Director and she assumed the mantle in the 2000-2001 Season. In 2005 the job of Managing Artistic Director was split into two positions because the Theatre had reached the point that two people were required to manage the business and artistic affairs of HCT, and John Rambo was welcomed as Managing Director.

The production quality at HCT has been recognized on the regional and state level, with actors and HCT receiving numerous awards from the Metrolina Theatre Association, The North Carolina Theatre Conference, and the Southeastern Theatre Conference. 

In 2007, the Theatre added two new programs for specific age groups. The RugBug Theatre is dedicated to producing plays with youth actors, ages 7-14, performing for young audiences, as young as three years old. The Encore Players is a program for seniors that produces one production every season.

Capital improvements have been underway since 2012 and have yielded a restored and updated Jeffers Theatre, renovated restrooms on the main level, an updated, and flexible, performance space and concessions bar in the Firemen’s Kitchen, as well as beautifully updated restrooms on that lower level. In the 2017-2018 season, HCT unveiled a gorgeously expanded lobby area. Renovations to the actors’ rehearsal hall were begun in 2019 and completed in 2020.

Pam Livingstone retired in June 2020 and Eric Seale, a native of Lexington Kentucky, was chosen in a national search to become the third Artistic Director of HCT.

Eric joined HCT amid the 2020 Coronavirus Pandemic, when the theatre was unable to host patrons. Much of his first season with HCT was spent developing tech capabilities which lead to live streaming productions between October 2020 and March 2021, producing all titles and personally directing DISENCHANTED, FULLY COMMITTED, and THE WEIR along with a studio recorded version of A CHRISTMAS CAROL. With the launching of the 73rd season Eric finally got to make his proper Hickory directorial debut with the musical comedy SOMETHING ROTTEN.

name: Aiken Community Theatre
bio:
The Aiken Community Theatre
Established in 1952, Aiken Community Playhouse was formed by a small group of community members with a common goal of providing entertainment for Aiken residents. Since then, the theatre relocated to a beautiful new facility, strengthened and expanded youth and educational programs, moved into a year-round entertainment production schedule, and rebranded as Aiken Community Theatre (ACT). ACT is a vital and ever-expanding hub of the arts in our community.

ACT is a nonprofit organization whose purpose is to entertain, educate, and enrich our community by providing a quality theatre experience. ACT is funded in part by the South Carolina Arts Commission which receives support from the National Endowment for the Arts.

name: Theatre In The Park
bio:
Over 70 Years of Engaging Performances

Theatre In The Park, located in the northern end of Raleigh’s scenic Pullen Park, is internationally acclaimed for its outstanding theatrical achievements, with more than 30,000 people attending our programming last year alone.

Originally chartered in 1947, Theatre In The Park started out as The Children’s Theatre of Raleigh, Inc. During the early 70s, the name was changed to Theatre In The Park in order to reflect its expanded programming, location, and new “home” in The National Guard Armory building located in Pullen Park. In 2004, the Raleigh City Council unanimously voted to rename the building as the “Ira David Wood III Pullen Park Theatre” to reflect the decades of work done by Artistic and Executive Director, Ira David Wood III.

The beautiful gardens outside Theatre In The Park are lovingly maintained by John S. Bento, whom the garden is named for. A fountain was erected in the garden, with the unanimous vote of the City Council, recognizing and memorializing former Raleigh Mayor Isabella Cannon.

Mission Statement

The mission of Theatre In The Park is to provide a quality theatre experience to a diverse audience base in Raleigh and the surrounding areas. Further, to offer the public an opportunity to see and participate in high quality dramatic classes and productions. Theatre In The Park’s mission also includes involving the community in the creation and development of live theatre to nurture a general appreciation and respect for the arts.

name: Theatre Charlotte
bio:
Theatre Charlotte is a volunteer-based theatre company dedicated to creating outstanding theatre opportunities that are accessible and relevant to the people of the Charlotte region.

Theatre Charlotte is committed to making theatre relevant in the lives of more people by demonstrating that theatre engages, inspires, and unites communities. Hundreds of volunteers get involved each year as actors, crew members, and ushers, while thousands participate as audience members. We encourage individuals of all ages and experiences to be a part of our productions and learn from our professional directors, designers, and staff.

Theatre Charlotte is proud of our heritage and excited about our future!

name: Camel City Playhouse
bio:
Our mission is to provide an amazing theatrical experience for diverse audiences while supporting our fellow artistic organizations and offering an open and welcoming event space.

Meet the Team Behind the Scenes
In the past years, we have grown into a respected theatre company that strives to bring current plays to our audiences. We dare to touch on social issues that other companies shy from. We are a theatre company for the young at heart, run by the young…and not so young.

name: Chapin Theatre Company
bio:
Experience the heart of live performance right here in your community. Grab a seat, grab a friend, and enjoy the show.

Whether you're in the audience cheering us on or backstage helping build the magic, there is a place for you here.

See What's Happening


Feel the Magic.
Join us for our upcoming Mary Poppins! [G] You won't want to miss this magical show.

name: Opera House Theatre Company
bio:
Inspiring artists and audiences since 1985
A theatre company committed to supporting, nurturing, and developing a rich array of local talent and the arts community in Wilmington, North Carolina. We are proud to be celebrating 41 years of live theatre!

Since 1985, Opera House Theatre Company has enriched Wilmington’s arts scene by producing high-quality live theater and nurturing local talent. Through its blend of professional guest artists and local performers, OHTC provides a platform for actors, musicians, and technicians to grow alongside industry professionals. Each year, it presents a dynamic season of musicals and educational programs, fostering creativity across generations and inspiring audiences through the transformative power of live theater. Rooted in the legacy of founders Lou Criscuolo and Mary James Morgan, OHTC remains committed to sustaining a vibrant arts community in Wilmington.

name: Cape Fear Regional Theatre
bio:
CFRT’s five-show mainstage season and robust education and outreach programs serve over 62,000 audience members a year from all ages and varying socioeconomic and ethnic backgrounds including over 22,000 students from around the region.

CFRT is a 501(c)3 not-for-profit organization.

name: Theatre of Dare
bio:
Community Theater for The Outer Banks
Theatre of Dare began in 1991 with the help of Ruth Ambrosius and Pat Clayton with the Outer Banks Forum. The first organizational meeting was held in November of that year and along with the Dare County Arts Council "TOD" was born. Actually the original (and mercifully brief) name of Theatre of Dare was the "Players of Truth and Dare"!

Auditions for the first production, California Suite, were held in January 1992 and the show was performed at the Port O'Call restaurant March 19-22, 1992, to great acclaim and gustatory delight. After a few other interesting locations were tried, the Theatre finally settled in the College of the Albemarle (formerly Manteo Middle School) auditorium, which had appropriate seating and a real theatrical stage... until 2017 when the auditorium was closed and torn down. Between 2017 and 2022, Theatre of Dare was a theatre 'on the run', performing in locations such as the Lost Colony Sound Stage, the Dare County Arts Council, Festival Park, and the Elizabethan Gardens. Finally, in 2022, almost thirty years to the day of our first production, Theatre of Dare opened its own place in Kitty Hawk, creating a brand new space for the performing arts in Dare County. 

Over the decades, TOD has performed dozens of major plays, musicals, and second stage vignettes. Each season brings more talent and energy to each production and we welcome with mosh pit enthusiasm assistance of every type, from hammer-wielding set builders to shy, undiscovered talent, often discovered after a misplaced hammer blow to the thumb.

So come on in and click away and then contact us to find out how the Theatre of Dare can be fun for you too!

name: May River Theatre
bio:
MISSION: May River Theatre is a nonprofit organization committed to engaging the Bluffton community through a breadth of quality theatrical performances that facilitate growth in both the production and understanding of the entire theatrical experience.

VISION: May River Theatre is the area community theatre that performers seek out when looking for productions that both challenge and showcase their full abilities, that new community members become involved in to build lasting relationships, and finally, MRT is the area community theatre that patrons attend who are interested in being entertained and challenged by a breadth of traditional and contemporary productions.

name: Flowertown Players
bio: Located in downtown Summerville at the historic James F. Dean theatre.

name: Florence Little Theatre
bio: The mission of the Florence Little Theatre is to provide excellence in theatrical entertainment and education in a safe and respectful environment while encouraging community involvement and support. Founded in 1923 as The Community Players, FLT is one of South Carolina's oldest continuously operating community theatres and celebrated its 100th anniversary in 2023. It has received the South Carolina Theatre of Distinction Award, the Elizabeth O'Neill Verner Award, and multiple South Carolina Arts Alliance honors, and runs youth education programs including the Schoolhouse Players, Children's Workshop, Rising Stars, and Summer Camp alongside its regular season.

name: Sumter Little Theatre
bio: Sumter Little Theatre has been Sumter, South Carolina's hometown community theatre for over 85 years, offering theatre classes and live performances that celebrate local talent. SLT produces a mainstage season of plays and musicals alongside a la carte community offerings, and supports a Youth Theatre education program. The theatre is committed to accessibility, offering wheelchair-accessible seating, hearing assistance, and a 'Pay What You Can' performance for every mainstage production so that cost is never a barrier to live theatre.

name: Swamp Fox Players
bio: Founded in 1971 by James and Ann Israel, the Swamp Fox Players began performing at the old Winyah High School Auditorium before touring to hotels, restaurants, state parks, and school auditoriums under the slogan 'Have Stage Will Travel.' In 1982, the group purchased the historic Strand Theater on Front Street, a former movie house built in 1941, and converted it into their permanent home. Now in its sixth decade, the Swamp Fox Players is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit that produces a full season of plays and musicals each year, run entirely by a volunteer Board of Directors and Production Committee, and remains a cornerstone of Georgetown County's cultural life.

name: Theatre of the Republic
bio: Founded in 1969, Theatre of the Republic (TOR) has been the official theatre of Horry County by legislative designation since 1975, bringing live musicals, plays, and special events to Conway's historic downtown Main Street district for over 50 years. TOR's mission is to be a major cultural resource by providing affordable, quality theatre with diversity in its programming, casts, and production crews, fostering inclusiveness across racial, gender, religious, socio-economic, age, and orientation lines. The season includes a Broadway Series mainstage lineup alongside Coastal Youth Theatre (CYT) productions for young performers.

name: Marlboro Players Community Theatre
bio: The Marlboro Players are the resident community theatre troupe performing at the Marlboro Civic Center, a 320-seat historic performing arts venue in downtown Bennettsville. Originally built in 1917 as The Garden Theater — one of the finest opera houses in the Carolinas — the building hosted vaudeville and traveling musical productions before becoming a movie house. After years of dormancy, it was restored through a public/private partnership and reopened in November 1995. Now on the National Register of Historic Places, the Civic Center hosts theatrical productions, concerts, and community events, drawing on a deep well of local talent.

name: Pine Tree Players
bio: The Pine Tree Players began as Fairfield Community Theater in 1972, originally performing in the Mt. Zion auditorium. In 1984, the Players renovated a former Mormon church — purchased by five Winnsboro businessmen and deeded to the group on the condition it operate as a 501(c)(3) — into the 88-seat Pine Tree Playhouse. For over fifty years, the Players have offered a wide range of classic, eclectic, and new works, averaging about five productions a year, including musicals, non-musicals, and original works by local authors, serving Fairfield County and the greater Columbia, SC area.

name: Greenville Theatre
bio: Founded in 1926 as the Greenville Little Theatre, this is the Upstate's oldest and largest locally producing professional theatre company and the first arts organization founded in the region. Originally an all-volunteer group performing at the Greenville Women's College, the company moved into its current home on Heritage Green in 1967 and returned to its original name, Greenville Theatre, in 2019. Under Producing Artistic Director Max Quinlan — formerly Resident Director of the 2014 Broadway revival of Les Misérables and the National Tour of The Phantom of the Opera — Greenville Theatre has produced some of its top-selling shows ever, including White Christmas, Mamma Mia!, and Anastasia. The theatre offers a full mainstage season alongside GT on Tour, Junior Players, camps, and educational programming for young audiences across the Upstate.

name: Centre Stage
bio: Founded in 1983 by Douglas P. McCoy, Centre Stage is South Carolina's only professional thrust-stage theatre — a year-round, 285-seat regional venue in downtown Greenville producing a full season of musicals, contemporary plays, comedies, and dramas. A Constituent Member of Theatre Communications Group and the Professional Division of the Southeastern Theatre Conference, Centre Stage also runs an annual New Play Festival and Fringe Series highlighting new and emerging work, including original musicals developed locally. Under Executive Artistic Director Laura Nicholas (since 2020), the theatre has produced numerous regional and world premieres while maintaining deep partnerships with the Metropolitan Arts Council and area colleges and universities.

name: The Warehouse Theatre
bio: Founded in 1973 when Furman University professor Dr. Peter Smith and Greenville Arts Council director Jim Boivin organized a summer theatre workshop for kids, The Warehouse Theatre grew out of a black box space converted from an annex of the Greenville Memorial Auditorium. The theatre moved to its current home in a renovated former cotton warehouse in 1998, becoming the cornerstone of Greenville's historic West End arts district. Today, The Warehouse Theatre is Greenville's only fully professional producing theatre and one of just two SPT (Small Professional Theatre) companies in South Carolina holding a contract with Actors' Equity Association. Beyond its six-to-seven-show Main Stage season, the theatre produces the free Upstate Shakespeare Festival each summer in Falls Park (over 60 productions since 1995), and runs a robust educational program including the This Wooden O language arts touring program, an Applied Theatre program, and community forum initiatives. Its stated mission is to be Upstate SC's premier professional theatre where community engagement and education complement thought-provoking theatre experiences.

name: Spartanburg Little Theatre
bio: Founded in 1945 when a group of Spartanburg residents met at the Cleveland Hotel to form a literary club, the organization became the Little Theatre of Spartanburg the following year, staging its first one-act play in 1946. In 1949, the Spartanburg County Foundation leased the group a former Camp Croft movie theater for one dollar a year; the company later became the first non-professional theatre permitted to stage a Rodgers and Hammerstein musical (Allegro, 1953, followed by Carousel). The County Foundation deeded the Camp Croft building to the theatre outright in 1978, naming it the David W. Reid Playhouse in 1982. In September 2007, after more than 50 years at Camp Croft, the company moved into the newly built Chapman Cultural Center, where it remains today. Spartanburg Little Theatre is largely volunteer-run, retaining a small professional staff and bringing in guest directors, musical directors, musicians, and choreographers as needed. It sponsors the Spartanburg Youth Theatre, the second-oldest youth theatre program in South Carolina, founded in 1973. In 2020, the South Carolina Theatre Association named Spartanburg Little Theatre a recipient of its Theatre of Distinction Award.

name: Carteret Community Theatre
bio: Founded in 1948, Carteret Community Theatre began as a small amateur group and has grown into a lasting cultural institution in Carteret County, producing over 300 major productions across comedies, dramas, large-scale musicals, and children's shows. The theatre has staged historical productions inspired by regional figures like Blackbeard and Otway Burns alongside popular musicals and family-friendly performances. It established a permanent home at 1311 Arendell Street in Morehead City in 2015. After several years away from its home venue, the theatre is celebrating a comeback season in 2026 with a newly renovated space. As a 501(c)(3) nonprofit, Carteret Community Theatre also runs youth arts education programs, including partnerships with the Missoula Children's Theatre program and the LeRae Kesel Fund, supporting young performers throughout the community.

name: New Bern Civic Theatre
bio: Founded in 1968, New Bern Civic Theatre (NBCT) has served as a vital artistic resource for Craven County and the surrounding Inner Banks/Coastal NC region for over 50 years. In 1980, the nonprofit purchased the then-vacant Athens Theatre, a beautifully restored downtown building originally built in 1910-1911 that showcased silent films, vaudeville, and traveling theatrical troupes in its early history, and staged its first production there that September, Neil Simon's Star Spangled Girl. In 1981, NBCT purchased the neighboring Athens Cafe Building at 412 Pollock Street, which was renovated in 2022 and is now used as a secondary rehearsal and event space called The Studio. Today NBCT is run by a 12-member board alongside more than 500 active volunteers, staging a regular season of plays, musicals, and youth theatre productions, along with classes, concerts, and special community events.

name: Thalian Association Community Theatre
bio: Believed by its own members since at least 1858 to date back to 1788, Thalian Association Community Theatre is widely considered the oldest theatre company in North Carolina and possibly the oldest still active in the United States, though rival claims from other historic companies make that distinction hard to prove definitively. The Association takes its name from Thalia, the Greek goddess of comedy. Its home, Thalian Hall, was built in 1858 on the same downtown Wilmington site as the Association's earlier venue, the 'Old Academy,' and today the Hall is owned and operated by the City of Wilmington while the theatre company itself operates as a separate, subscription-based membership organization. In an unbroken run dating to 1929, the Association has produced five plays and musicals each season on Thalian Hall's main stage. It also founded a Youth Theatre program in 1979, has managed the Hannah Block Historic USO/Community Arts Center for the City of Wilmington since 1994, and originated the Orange Street ArtsFest visual arts festival in 1995. In 2007, the North Carolina Senate officially proclaimed Thalian Association Community Theatre the Official Community Theatre of North Carolina.

name: Jacksonville Performing Arts Company
bio: Jacksonville Performing Arts Company (JPAC) bills itself as the first-ever 'Boutique Theater' in the United States, designed to create a more immersive, intimate experience for its patrons and a warm family atmosphere for performers and audiences alike. The company emphasizes building confidence, self-esteem, and friendship among its casts, ensuring every actor gets a genuine moment to shine rather than being relegated to the background. JPAC runs a free Teen Outreach program and a School of the Arts youth program for ages 5-15, works closely with performers on the autism spectrum and with disabilities, and has donated thousands of dollars to community causes including the USO of North Carolina's Jacksonville Center and local charity The Blessing Shed. The company partners with the City of Jacksonville Recreation & Parks for a free Summer Cultural Art series at the Jacksonville Amphitheater, with the Onslow County Public Library for an annual immersive Renaissance Faire, and with the Theaters at MCCS Camp Lejeune-New River to bring free Broadway-style shows to the military community. JPAC has been featured on FOX, CBS, and NBC, and in Voyager Magazine Raleigh.

name: Flat Rock Playhouse
bio: Flat Rock Playhouse traces its roots to 1937, when a group of struggling performers led by Robroy Farquhar organized as the Vagabond Players, eventually settling in the Blue Ridge region of Western North Carolina by 1940 and staging their first summer season in a converted 150-year-old grist mill called The Old Mill Playhouse at Highland Lake. After stints at Lake Summit following WWII, the troupe purchased an 8-acre lot in the Village of Flat Rock in 1952, giving rise to the Flat Rock Playhouse itself. In 1961, the North Carolina General Assembly officially designated it The State Theatre of North Carolina. What began as a few weeks of summer performances now spans a nine-month season of plays, Broadway musicals, comedy, drama, and theatre for young audiences, drawing more than 100,000 patrons annually and serving as a significant contributor to the local economy and the arts across North Carolina. The Playhouse also runs a professional apprentice and intern program alongside year-round classes for students from kindergarten through adulthood.

name: Asheville Community Theatre
bio: Asheville Community Theatre traces its founding to June 9, 1946, when a newspaper ad invited the community to form a theatre together, merging The Asheville Little Theater, The Players Guild, and the Asheville Theater Guild. The organization marks its official birthday as July 17, 1946, the day of its first membership campaign, and opened its very first production, Dark of the Moon, on August 17, 1946. A young Charlton Heston and his wife Lydia Clarke arrived from New York shortly after to co-direct ACT's third production and several more, including the theatre's first-ever non-professional performance of The Glass Menagerie; Heston later credited his time at ACT as pivotal to his decision to pursue acting professionally. Now approaching its 80th season, Asheville Community Theatre is the oldest continuously operating theatre in Asheville and the second-oldest in North Carolina, running a full Mainstage season alongside Youth Productions, a Readers Theatre Showcase, ACT Late Night, a Summer Play Series, and extensive youth education programs including the Tanglewood Troupes.

name: Haywood Arts Regional Theatre (HART)
bio: Founded in 1984, HART Theatre (Haywood Arts Regional Theatre) is a 501(c)(3) semi-professional community theatre nestled in the shadow of Cold Mountain in Waynesville, showcasing talent from the region and beyond. Its Performing Arts Center opened in 1997 on the eight-acre National Historic site of the Shelton House Museum of North Carolina Handicrafts, built in the style of a traditional 1920s Summer Stock playhouse. A 2016 expansion added the flexible Fangmeyer Theater, and the complex now houses three distinct performance spaces: the 255-seat Lloyd Main Stage inside the James Auditorium, the 140-seat Fangmeyer Theater, and the 75-seat Feichter Studio Theatre. HART has been named North Carolina Community Theatre of the Year, is a three-time N.C. Theatre Festival AACT/Fest winner and two-time Southeastern Theatre Festival AACT/Fest winner, and has even participated in the Edinburgh Scotland International Theatre Fringe Festival. Beyond its own productions, HART hosts events for Folkmoot USA, the Smoky Mountain Brass Band, and Voices in the Laurel, operates the Rodwell Visual Arts Gallery, and runs an Academy at HART youth program alongside internships for aspiring young theatre professionals.

name: Sandhills Repertory Theatre
bio: Sandhills Repertory Theatre (SRT) was born when NYC actor and occupational therapist Michael Pizzi moved to Pinehurst and discovered there were no professional musical theatre offerings in Moore County. After connecting with the O'Neal School, which had a 250-seat theatre with a stage well-suited to small-cast professional musical theatre and cabaret-style shows, Pizzi began bringing Broadway performers to the Sandhills to perform themed songbook concerts and revues celebrating composers and legends like Burt Bacharach, Tony Bennett, and Andrew Lloyd Webber. SRT is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit, and a percentage of net profits from every show goes toward the Sandhills Theatre Arts in the Schools (STARTS) fund, which supports performing arts programs in Moore County schools.

name: Temple Theatre Company
bio: Built in 1925 as a Vaudeville house, Temple Theatre stands as a monument to Sanford's artistic history. Nearly a century ago, the theatre was a stop for New York-based theatre troupes passing through on their way to Florida, thanks to its convenient location near the railroad station. As the railroad era faded, the building transformed to fit the community's needs, becoming a movie theatre, a furniture store, and a men's clothing outlet before closing in 1965. In 1981, the son of the theatre's original owner led a community restoration effort, securing National Historic Site registration and a grant from the North Carolina Legislature, and the theatre reopened in 1984 with much of its original architecture intact. Now billed as 'Central Carolina's Center for the Performing Arts,' Temple Theatre provides professional, high-quality productions year-round alongside extensive youth education programs (including Temple Academy, a Summer Conservatory, and the Temple Teen Ensemble) and a wide range of special events.

name: Harnett Regional Theatre
bio: Harnett Regional Theatre (HRT) is a 501(c)(3) community theatre based at the historic Stewart Theater in Downtown Dunn, whose mission is to educate and entertain by providing the opportunity for participation in high quality theatre for the people of Harnett County and the surrounding areas. HRT is currently celebrating its 50th anniversary season. Beyond its regular mainstage productions, the theatre runs a summer workshop for students ages 10-16 that culminates in a public performance, and its work is supported in part by the North Carolina Arts Council, a division of the state's Department of Natural and Cultural Resources.

name: The Theatre at the Rocky Mount Imperial Centre
bio: The Imperial Centre for the Arts & Sciences is a 135,000-square-foot cultural facility in downtown Rocky Mount, built on the site of the former Imperial Tobacco Company after Hurricane Floyd destroyed the city's previous downtown Children's Museum, Arts Center, and community Playhouse theater in September 1999. Opened in 2005, the Imperial Centre now houses the Maria V. Howard Arts Center, a Children's Museum & Science Center, a planetarium, and the Theatre — a community theatre program that has served Rocky Mount for more than 70 years, staging comedies, dramas, musicals, and children's theatre with an all-volunteer cast and crew.

name: Playhouse of Wilson
bio: The Playhouse of Wilson is a non-profit, community-based theatre group in Wilson, NC, whose mission is to provide the local community with enjoyable theatre experiences while offering opportunities to all who desire to support production and performance through time, talent, and gifts. The Playhouse stages its mainstage productions at the Edna Boykin Cultural Center in historic downtown Wilson, a venue it shares with several other local arts organizations.

name: Greenville Theatre Arts Center (GTAC)
bio: Founded in 1992 by Annette Campbell in Greenville, NC, the Greenville Theatre Arts Center (GTAC) is a private nonprofit foundation focused on artistic healing through the performing, creative, applied, visual, and musical arts, with an emphasis on serving individuals and communities affected by trauma and systemic injustice. Rather than staging a traditional annual season of scripted productions, GTAC's primary programming centers on youth development, including its Annual Summer Performing Arts Camp for ages 8-17, which culminates in an original student-created production developed collaboratively during the camp.

name: Smiles and Frowns Playhouse
bio: Smiles and Frowns Playhouse is a nonprofit organization dedicated to producing live children's theatre in Pitt County, NC, with the tagline 'theatre for children, by children.' Founded in 1986, the Playhouse has introduced the art form to several thousand young people across grades K-12, who both perform on stage and work behind the scenes on every production. The organization stages two shows a year — one in the fall and one in the spring — at the historic Doug Mitchell Auditorium within the Ayden Arts & Recreation Center, and also offers audition workshops to help young performers build confidence and audition skills. Smiles and Frowns also awards an annual scholarship, the Andrea Croskery Scholarship, to a graduating participant.

name: Children's Theatre of Charlotte
bio: Founded in 1948 by the Junior League of Charlotte as volunteer-run children's programming in the wake of World War II, Children's Theatre of Charlotte has grown into one of the most respected arts and education organizations in the country, now marking its 79th season. The Theatre's home, ImaginOn: The Joe and Joan Martin Center, opened in 2005 as a groundbreaking collaboration with Charlotte Mecklenburg Library, and features two performance spaces: the 550-seat McColl Family Theatre and the 250-seat Wells Fargo Playhouse. Beyond its professional Mainstage season, the Theatre operates the Tarradiddle Players resident touring company (est. 1989), an extensive School of Theatre Training program, a Resident Touring Company reaching schools across North Carolina and the Southeast, and The Kindness Project, an initiative launched in 2016 commissioning original plays for young audiences centered on kindness. Each season, the curtain rises more than 600 times for public, school, and touring performances, reaching more than 250,000 children, families, and educators annually.

name: Matthews Playhouse of the Performing Arts
bio: Founded in 1995 by June Bayless with a vision to give the community a place to experience and participate in the performing arts, Matthews Playhouse began as a small children's theatre — its first production, Alice in Wonderland, drew over 100 auditionees. After operating out of the Matthews Community Center, a temporary volunteer-built 100-seat theater, and back into the newly renovated Community Center by 2000, the Playhouse expanded in 2002 at the request of Mayor Lee Myers to include full-length adult and family productions, beginning with The Sound of Music. Now marking its 31st season, Matthews Playhouse is one of the largest theatre companies in the Charlotte region, running a five-show professional-quality Mainstage series alongside an extensive School of Theatre program, dinner theatre, sensory-friendly and Pay-What-You-Can performances, and summer camps serving over 1,000 children annually. The Playhouse has received numerous honors including the 2022 BroadwayWorld Charlotte Award for Favorite Local Theatre, 2024 Charlotte's Best Live Theater, and NCTC's 2024 Best Community Theatre in NC.

name: Bulldog Ensemble Theater
bio: Bulldog Ensemble Theater is a group of Durham artists who create productions of the best new American plays that speak to the local community. Inspired by the 30-year legacy of Durham's Manbites Dog Theater, where many of its members first came together, Bulldog works to cultivate artists and audiences for adventurous, of-the-moment material, including developing new plays by local writers and teaching theater arts classes for community members. Operating under the motto 'Of Durham, By Durham, For Durham,' the company's annual roster of artists reflects the city's demographics, with an ongoing commitment to recruiting the next generation of creative collaborators from across the region. Bulldog performs primarily at Mettlesome, a comedy and performance venue at the Golden Belt Campus in Durham.

name: North Raleigh Arts & Creative Theatre (NRACT)
bio: Founded in 2002 by Julianne Carson and her husband, North Raleigh Arts & Creative Theatre began as a children's teaching theatre in a small community center at Lake Lynn — with early rehearsals held in the founder's attic before the company outgrew its space and moved to its current location in the Greystone Shopping Center. What started with a production of Alice in Wonderland has since grown into a full nonprofit community theatre serving north Raleigh and the surrounding area, offering a regular season of mainstage productions alongside quality theatre education classes and camps for all ages. NRACT is funded in part by the City of Raleigh (via the Raleigh Arts Commission) and the North Carolina Arts Council.

name: Carolina Academy of Performing Arts (CAPA)
bio: Carolina Academy of Performing Arts (CAPA) is a premier educational organization providing conservatory-level instruction in theatre, music, dance, and film for youth ages 4-18 as well as adults. Founded by Melanie Prince, CAPA's instructors have professional Broadway, film, and television experience, and the academy operates in a supportive, non-competitive environment designed to challenge and inspire performers. CAPA has received national recognition from the iTheatrics International Junior Theater Festival, including honors for Excellence in Acting and Excellence in Dance. The academy stages student productions through its CAPA JR Production and Summer Stock Production programs, with past shows including Mamma Mia!, Matilda, Between the Lines, and The Willow in the Winds. Instruction is currently located at Hope Church in Apex.

name: PlayMakers Repertory Company
bio: Founded in 1976 as the successor to the historic Carolina Playmakers, PlayMakers Repertory Company is the professional theatre in residence at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, named for the university's Historic Playmakers Theatre. Now celebrating its 50th anniversary season, PlayMakers is widely regarded as North Carolina's premier professional theatre company, producing a mix of classics and some of the most exciting new plays in American theatre each season across two stages, alongside a Summer Youth Conservatory program culminating in a public production performed by high school students.

name: Cary Players Community Theatre Company
bio: Founded in 2001 by Dan Marchenko, Cary Players is the heartbeat of community theatre in Cary, North Carolina, entirely fueled by personal donations and corporate sponsorships. Now in its 22nd season, the all-volunteer company has brought over 70 productions to life spanning musicals and straight plays, guided by a set of core values: Inspire the Patron, Respect the Player, Uplift the Community, and Educate, Enlighten & Entertain. Cary Players performs at the Cary Arts Center and is committed to diversity, equity, and inclusion in its programming and casting.

name: Zingher Productions
bio: Zingher Productions is a theatre and film company founded by Jessica Zingher in 2023, legally registered in Cornelius, NC, and specializing in film and television production, theatre, and immersive experiences. The company focuses on bringing smart, funny, and often downright weird work to audiences — stories designed to leave viewers thinking all the way home. Zingher Productions' regional premiere of I'm Gonna Marry You Tobey Maguire marks a notable entry into the Charlotte-area/Lake Norman theatre scene, bringing an acclaimed off-off-Broadway hit (previously staged in New York and London) to local audiences.

name: Warehouse Performing Arts Center (Warehouse PAC)
bio: Warehouse Performing Arts Center began in 2008 when local property developer Jim Morton offered his daughter, Marla Brown, 1,500 square feet of unused office space off Westmoreland Road in Cornelius. Marla and collaborator Marshall Cesena, who met teaching a drama camp at Mt. Zion UMC and the Cornelius YMCA, gave the venture its tongue-in-cheek name — 'Performing Arts Center' in a converted warehouse office suite — and began as an informal salon where people gathered to read plays, share ideas, and take creative risks. As the company grew, Warehouse evolved into a full producing organization committed to thoughtful, high-quality theatrical work while treating artists like humans. After the pandemic disrupted operations (including the loss of their venue) and a period spent working in larger production environments, the team made an intentional decision to return home to Cornelius and rebuild something sustainable and personal. Today, Warehouse PAC operates out of an intimate 80-seat black box theatre, producing both 'Warehouse Signature Productions' (fully curated, professionally designed mainstage shows) and 'Warehouse Partner Productions' (community-based, collaborative programming emphasizing access and shared ownership).

name: Theatre Raleigh
bio: Theatre Raleigh grew out of 'Hot Summer Nights at the Kennedy' series, begun in 2005 by K.D. Kennedy Jr. and his son Michael Kennedy. In 2009, Lauren Kennedy Brady took over the series from her father and brother, building it into a year-round professional company and renaming it Theatre Raleigh. The organization officially incorporated as a nonprofit in 2013. In 2020, amid the COVID-19 pandemic, Theatre Raleigh moved out of its former home at Martin Marietta Center and built its own campus, Theatre Raleigh Arts Center, which now includes two buildings and four performance spaces. The company has since merged with Raleigh Act to create Theatre Raleigh ACT for youth education and performances, and opened The Green Room cafe on site. As a professional nonprofit theatre operating under Actors' Equity Association contracts, Theatre Raleigh produces Broadway-caliber work employing both local professionals and Broadway veterans, and has grown into one of the Triangle's top theatre destinations.

name: Center Theater Company
bio: Center Theater Company was founded in 2021 by Jenny Latimer, a Utah native who began performing professionally in New York City at age 17 and went on to originate the role of Cosette in the 25th Anniversary National Tour of Les Misérables. Moving from New York to North Carolina, Latimer opened Center Theater Company in a Carrboro space formerly occupied by The ArtsCenter, aiming to make the Chapel Hill/Carrboro area her artistic home. The company describes its work as 'both by kids and for kids,' running youth productions, a Conservatory training program, and summer camps alongside larger multi-generational community productions — including an annual holiday tradition, A Christmas Carol, now in its fourth year, and other family-friendly mainstage shows like The Sound of Music and The Secret Garden. Center Theater emphasizes building confidence and creativity in young performers while bringing the wider Carrboro/Chapel Hill community together through multi-generational casts.

name: Carolina Children's Theatre / Youth Arts Academy (CCT)
bio: Carolina Children's Theatre (CCT) is an award-winning youth theatre organization serving Fuquay-Varina, Holly Springs, Garner, Apex, Lillington, Angier, Willow Spring, and the greater Raleigh area. A WRAL Voter's Choice Award winner for Best Performance Venue, CCT's mission is to provide a safe, fun, and creative environment for children and families, blending global theatre, classic stories, and visual art with imagination to support young performers. The organization has staged familiar tales including Peter Pan, The Wizard of Oz, Around the World in 80 Days, Babes in Toyland, A Christmas Carol, and Mary Poppins Jr., alongside original productions written exclusively for CCT by founder Christina Cass Catton. CCT offers year-round drama classes, camps, and productions for ages 8-18, and participates in the iTheatrics International Junior Theater Festival. CCT recently relocated its rehearsal and class space to the American Legion, Building 2, at 6400 Johnson Pond Road in Fuquay-Varina, while performances are typically staged at the Fuquay-Varina Arts Center or Holly Springs Cultural Center.

name: Spiritual Twist Productions
bio: Spiritual Twist Productions (STP) is a nonprofit Christian theater and School of the Arts located in Garner, giving children and youth ages 4 through adult the opportunity to experience the performing arts within a Christian context and as a medium for Christian ministry. Located in the Raleigh area since 1987, STP describes itself as one of the Triangle's best-kept secrets, producing roughly 10-12 major musicals a year across multiple age-based casts (including dedicated youth and Adult Intensive casts). Their stated mission is to produce real musical theater with a spiritual twist, speaking truth and showing hope every time their performers take the stage, blending biblically-themed productions (such as retellings of Daniel, Samson, and other Scripture stories) alongside broader family and holiday programming.

name: Winston-Salem Theatre Alliance
bio: Winston-Salem Theatre Alliance was founded in 1983 by director Fred Gorelick, who taught advanced acting classes at the Little Theatre of Winston-Salem and began producing 'showcase' productions to display his students' work to the public. Under current Artistic Director Jamie Lawson, that original vision grew into a permanent, independently-operating theatre now celebrating its 44th season. The Alliance's mission is to inspire, transform, and unite the people of the Triad through a broad range of unique, diverse, and unconventional theatrical experiences. Known for staging titles rarely seen on other community theatre stages in the region, the Alliance produces an unusually prolific schedule — often 20+ productions a year — across three distinct venues within its downtown facility: the main Jamie Lawson Auditorium/Ihrie Theatre, the intimate Beall black-box theatre, and the outdoor Gray Smith Stage. The organization also runs Shine Theatre Camp and TA's rising sTArs, a program spotlighting younger performers.

name: Alamance Children's Theatre (ACT)
bio: Established in 1980, Alamance Children's Theatre (ACT) is a private, nonprofit community-based organization providing theatrical opportunities for youth ages 8 through 18, both on stage and behind the scenes. A member group of Alamance Arts (formerly the Alamance County Arts Council), ACT is partially supported by the GRASSROOTS program of the North Carolina Arts Council. ACT presents three full-scale productions each season, typically at the Paramount Theater in downtown Burlington (though occasionally at other regional venues such as the Mebane Arts Convention Center), with casts generally consisting of 35-40 actors plus backstage youth technical staff. ACT also offers ACT II, a program providing additional acting challenges for older or more experienced youth actors, hosts theater workshops throughout the year on topics like auditioning and character development, and runs ACTing Up, a summer performing arts camp for ages 7-14 aimed primarily at newer performers.

name: Old Courthouse Theatre (OCT)
bio: Founded in 1976 by Mary Snead Boger, Old Courthouse Theatre (OCT) is a cornerstone of the Concord, North Carolina arts scene, now celebrating its 51st season. Located in a beautifully restored former church building over 100 years old, OCT blends the city's historic charm with vibrant theatrical expression. Each season, the theatre produces five mainstage shows (plays and musicals) alongside youth productions and numerous special events. OCT also supports emerging voices and experimental work through its Wilson Family Black Box space, home to the Living Room Reading Series, the annual 10-Minute Play Festival (now in its 15th season), Papa Capp's Variety Show, and resident company the Post Mortem Players. OCT is a proud member of the Metrolina Theatre Association, American Association of Community Theatre, Arts North Carolina, and the Cabarrus Chamber, and is supported in part by a Grassroots Arts Program grant from the North Carolina Arts Council, administered by the Cabarrus Arts Council.

name: Post Mortem Players
bio: Founded in 2022 by horror fan, Charlotte native, and long-time performing arts professional Chris Stonnell, Post Mortem Players is a theatre company specializing in stage works of horror, the macabre, and things that go bump in the night. Representing the greater Charlotte, North Carolina region, productions take place in the Wilson Family Black Box at Old Courthouse Theatre in Concord. Each season consists of three hair-raising productions: an annual 'Christmas Spirits' ghost story every December, plus two additional classic or contemporary horror plays or musicals — one for Halloween in October, and the other in late spring/early summer.

name: Lincoln Theatre Guild
bio: Formed in 1981 with just 15 members, Lincoln Theatre Guild's mission is to bring the passion of the performing arts to the Lincoln County, North Carolina area, providing quality live theatrical entertainment in a supportive environment for the enjoyment and education of the greater community. The Guild's first production was Harvey, and in 1988 the group moved its offices and productions to the Lincoln Cultural Center, a renovated former church in downtown Lincolnton. LTG presently produces 4-5 shows per year at the Cultural Center, along with occasional performances at the North Lincoln High School auditorium, and runs a popular annual Elementary and Teen Drama Camp each summer culminating in public performances.

name: Footlight Players
bio: Founded in 1931, Footlight Players is Charleston's original theatre company, now marking its 95th season. In residence at the historic Queen Street Playhouse in downtown Charleston, the all-volunteer, nonprofit company has staged hundreds of productions spanning nearly a century, offering the Lowcountry a full MainStage season of comedies, dramas, and musicals each year alongside seasonal specialty shows. Recent seasons have included acclaimed productions of Cabaret and Amadeus. Footlight Players' Season 95 leans heavily into comedy, featuring the regional premiere of Dracula: A Comedy of Terrors alongside classic and contemporary crowd-pleasers.

name: Southern Wake Players
bio: Southern Wake Players is the community theater program operated by the Holly Springs Cultural Center, a Town of Holly Springs, NC facility. The group stages public theatrical productions at the Cultural Center, which it shares with the town's public library.

name: Main Stage Community Theatre
bio: Founded in the early 1990s, Main Stage Community Theatre is a nonprofit dedicated to providing live theater experiences for both youth and adults across Hilton Head Island, Bluffton, and the surrounding Lowcountry. With a mission to 'engage the artist in anyone, inspire the artist in everyone,' the theatre produces between two and four full-scale shows annually, casting local talent ranging from roughly seven to eighteen years old alongside adult performers, and often stages productions at rotating venues including Coligny Theatre, Hilton Head Prep's Main Street Theatre, and area high school auditoriums. Recent and past productions have included Newsies, Bye Bye Birdie, The Addams Family, All Shook Up, Shrek, and Beauty and the Beast. Attendance exceeds 5,000 annually, and the theatre also offers education programs and a summer camp for young performers.

name: Theatre Statesville
bio: Bringing stories to life in Iredell County since 1958, Theatre Statesville is a volunteer-based, nonprofit organization offering quality live theatre, lifelong learning opportunities, and creative expression throughout the Greater Iredell community. Its mission is to enrich the community through exceptional theatre that inspires, educates, and connects, serving as a vibrant anchor for the performing arts by empowering local artists and fostering inclusive partnerships across all ages. Recent programming has included the 2025 world premiere of Mississippi Queens alongside a full season of family and adult-oriented productions.

name: Ferry Tales Youth Theater
bio: Ferry Tales Youth Theater began in 2021 with a simple idea: giving local children more opportunities to experience the performing arts close to home. After a local all-ages community theater production wrapped up, parents began asking what would come next for their kids, leading to a summer camp for young performers and, eventually, a weekly theater club. Named as a playful nod to its hometown of Sneads Ferry, the organization officially secured 501(c)(3) nonprofit status and now produces a wide range of shows, showcases, and camps each year — recent titles include Matilda: The Musical, Junie B. Jones Jr., Honk!, Finding Nemo Jr., and Footloose: Youth Edition. Its mission is to promote literacy and provide access to the fine arts within Onslow County, North Carolina and its neighboring communities.

name: The Freedom Players Youth Theatre Group
bio: The Freedom Players Youth Theatre Group is a dynamic program of The Cultivator, a Hertford County nonprofit dedicated to promoting rural literacy, food access, creativity, and storytelling. The group welcomes young people from all backgrounds — homeschooled, private, or public school students alike — and brings them to the stage through a yearly summer camp program and regular theatre practices, fostering inclusivity and a sense of belonging. Since debuting with The Wizard of Oz and The Addams Family: Young At Part in 2023, the Freedom Players have gone on to stage The Outsiders, Matilda Jr., Willy Wonka Jr., The Great Gatsby, Charlotte's Web, The Sound of Music, and Beetlejuice Jr. The group has been featured in EdNC, the Roanoke-Chowan News-Herald, and Spectrum News 1 for its work using theatre to cultivate imagination, teamwork, confidence, and community connection in rural northeastern North Carolina.

name: The Justice Theater Project
bio: In 2004, community members at St. Francis of Assisi Catholic Church produced A Lesson Before Dying to advocate for those facing the death penalty. What was meant to be a single performance became a local tour and eventually its own entity: The Justice Theater Project. Now marking over 20 years in the Triangle, JTP produces compelling theater experiences that create community dialogue and give voice to social concerns, connecting, inspiring, and impacting the community through engaging performing arts outreach, education, and advocacy. The company's programming often draws on documentary and verbatim theatre techniques, tackling subjects like immigration, criminal justice, and civil rights, alongside classic dramas and musicals with a social-justice lens. JTP also runs summer camps for kids and is funded in part by the City of Raleigh, the North Carolina Arts Council, and the United Arts Council of Raleigh and Wake County.

name: Different Strokes! Performing Arts Collective
bio: Different Strokes! Performing Arts Collective is an Asheville, NC theatre company dedicated to 'Making Theater That Makes a Difference.' Under Managing Artistic Director Stephanie Hickling Beckman, the company produces a mix of world premieres, workshop productions of new works, staged reading series, and its long-running 369 Monologue and Short Play Festival, often centering stories of race, identity, resilience, and cultural diversity. Programming has included the INK of our KIN staged reading series celebrating Black playwrights, original one-person shows, and new dramas developed by local and touring artists. The company is supported by ArtsAVL, Buncombe County Government, and the North Carolina Arts Council.

name: Scrap Paper Shakespeare
bio: Scrap Paper Shakespeare is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit theatre company producing accessible classical theatre in the NC Triangle since 2022. Named for the idea that big ideas can come from the humblest components — a scrap of paper is all it takes to capture something great — the company stages the works of William Shakespeare, lesser-performed classical plays, and original works inspired by classic stories. Its mission centers on the belief that classical theatre can and should be accessible, whether you're a Shakespeare pro or slept through high school English class. Beyond its mainstage season, Scrap Paper Shakespeare runs a free educational touring program bringing 60-minute Shakespeare adaptations to families, and hosts Much Fear Shakespeare, an annual audience-interactive fundraiser where patrons can heckle and sabotage the actors mid-performance.

name: Alleghany Community Theatre (ACT)
bio: Established in 2000, Alleghany Community Theatre (ACT) is a small, entirely volunteer-powered community theatre in the Blue Ridge Mountains of Sparta, North Carolina, with a reputation built over more than 30 years of local performances. Rather than operating out of one dedicated venue, ACT stages its productions across a variety of locations throughout Alleghany County and neighboring communities, from local auditoriums to venues like the Burgiss Barn at Thistle Meadow Winery in Laurel Springs. The company produces 1-3 mainstage shows per year alongside 3-4 readers theatre productions, with a mission to promote appreciation of live theatre while increasing knowledge and providing an outlet for creative arts in the community. Scripts for upcoming shows are often made available for perusal at the Alleghany County Public Library ahead of auditions.

name: Brunswick Little Theatre
bio: Founded in 1983 when three friends — Patricia Foy, Stuart Callari, and Gloria Yount — discovered their shared love of theatre over a glass of wine, Brunswick Little Theatre (BLT) is an all-volunteer, nonprofit organization dedicated to creating awareness and appreciation of the performing arts in the greater Brunswick County, North Carolina area. The company's first production, Brigadoon, was staged in 1983 at the Hatch Auditorium at the Baptist Assembly on Caswell Beach; BLT performed at various venues around Southport for decades before leasing its current home, a converted former church building, in 2014, and finally purchasing the property outright by 2018 through a dedicated capital campaign ('The 100 Club'). BLT now stages a full annual season of plays, farces, dramas, and musicals, plus mystery dinner theatres, Halloween escape rooms, poetry readings, and educational programs, including popular Music Theatre Apprentice classes for young performers.

name: Montford Park Players (MPP)
bio: Founded by Hazel Robinson in 1973 with a production of As You Like It performed in Asheville's Montford neighborhood, Montford Park Players (MPP) is North Carolina's longest-running Shakespeare theatre company. Performances moved to their permanent outdoor home in 1983, when the City of Asheville and U.S. Navy Construction Battalion terraced a hillside near Riverside Cemetery, creating what would later be renamed the Hazel Robinson Amphitheatre in the founder's honor. MPP is one of only 15 theatres worldwide to have staged every single one of Shakespeare's plays, and annually records the third-highest attendance of any outdoor theatre in North Carolina, behind The Lost Colony and Unto These Hills. All performances are completely free, offered on a pay-what-you-can donation basis, with a mission of making theatre accessible to everyone regardless of financial means. Beyond its summer Shakespeare season, MPP presents an annual holiday production of A Christmas Carol, runs Montford Moppets (a youth theatre-in-residence program), and involves roughly 200 volunteer members annually.

name: The Gilbert Theater
bio: Founded in 1994 by Lynn Pryer in the basement of his own home, The Gilbert Theater has grown into a semi-professional, community-minded company providing quality contemporary and classical theatrical productions in downtown Fayetteville, NC. Named in honor of the Marquis de Lafayette, the theater moved through several downtown locations before settling into its current home on the second floor of the Fascinate-U Children's Museum. The Gilbert has staged work by noted playwrights including Donald Margulies, Eve Ensler, Suzan-Lori Parks, Paula Vogel, Christopher Durang, Athol Fugard, and Moisés Kaufman, alongside original local and regional plays. Since Robyne Parrish became Artistic Director in 2012, the company has hired a small percentage of union actors and professional designers, launched the Gilbert Conservatory, the Gilbert Rep, and the Gilbert Glee Club, and built a strong volunteer base through the Gilbert Guild.
